The facts of the case:-
The Complainant initiated private complaint under Section 200 of Cr.P.C., against the Accused for the offence punishable under Sec.138 of Negotiable Instruments Act on the ground that the Accused got introduced to the Complainant through a car dealer while selling his car, after purchasing the car Mahindra Scorpio from the Complainant developed friendship with the Complainant and understood Complainant's entire background and started expressing his financial inconsistency in his Borewell digging business and offered the Complainant a partnership in his existing Borewelll digging business known as Shri Navadurga Borewell and induced him to invest Rs.40,00,000/- as Complainant's share under the terms and condition mentioned therein and after receiving Rs.40,00,000/- through Cheque bearing No.646275 dtd. 5.8.2013 with Complainant inter alia agreeing to conduct the said business under the terms and conditions agreed thereunder.
It is further stated by the Complainant that, on 4.9.2013, the Accused had issued a Cheque bearing No.363559 drawn ICICI Bank, Kammanahalli branch, Bengaluru for Rs.1,00,000/- in favour of Complainant towards profit share of the said partnership, when the said Cheque got dishonoured for the reason "funds insufficient" and when the Complainant informed the same to the Accused, he had paid Rs.2,00,000/- in cash in small portions in installments.
It is further stated by the Complainant that, the on regular follow-ups with the Accused, the Complainant had received 04 Cheques towards profit share.
But the same were dishonoured for the reason "funds insufficient".
Thereafter, the Complainant had decided to end the business relationship with the Accused and demanded for return of his investment amount.

It is further stated that even after consistent followups with the Accused for payment of investment amount and finally decided to initiate legal action against the Accused and the Complainant approached the Accused for demanding payment.

It is further stated that, even after giving sufficient time for refunding the amount, the Accused had failed to make the payment and the Complainant deciding to initiate legal action and approaching to jurisdictional police station,
knowing this fact the Accused had immediately approached the Complainant and stopped him from lodging the Complainant and issued Cheques bearing No.385677 dtd. 4.7.2016 for Rs.14,00,000/-
and another Cheque bearing No.385690 dtd. 5.7.2016 for Rs.2,00,000/- both drawn on ICICI Bank,
Kammanahalli branch, Bengaluru in favour of Complainant with an assurance of honouring the same.

It is further submitted by the Complainant that believing the Accused, the Complainant presented the said Cheques for twice through his banker The Bangalore City Co-op. Bank, HRBR Layout Branch, Bengaluru on its due dates on 25.8.2016.
But the said Cheques were returned unpaid for there as on "funds insufficient" on 26.8.2016.
Thereafter he informed the same to the Accused.
Thereafter, the Complainant got issued demand notice to the Accused through RPAD on 23.9.2016 and sent on 24.9.2013 through his counsel.
But the same was returned with a shara 'door locked'.

Inspite of knowledge of legal notice, the Accused has neither paid the Cheques amount nor replied to the notice and thereby, the Accused has committed the offense punishable under Sec.138 of Negotiable Instruments Act.
Thereafter the Complainant approached the trial court for appropriate legal action against the accused.

12. Before re-appreciating the evidence on record, it is necessary to refer some of the latest rulings of the Hon'ble Apex Court reported in 2019 (3) KCCR 2473 (SC) (Basalingappa V/s Mudibasappa), the Hon'ble Apex Court while considering several earlier rulings on the offence U/Sec.138 of NI Act and also on the presumption U/ Sec.118 and 139 of NI Act, at Para 23 was pleased to observe as follows:
23.

We having noticed the ratio laid down by this Court in above cases on Sections 118(a) and 139, we now summarise the principles enumerated by this Court in following manner:-
(i) Once the execution of cheque is admitted Section 139 of the Act mandates a presumption that the cheque was for the discharge of any debt or other liability.

(ii) The presumption under Section 139 is a rebuttable Vijay Ananth vs Thomas Edenezer Sathiadass on 12 July, 2024 Indian Kanoon - http://indiankanoon.org/doc/149764968/
10 presumption and the onus is on the accused to raise the probable defence.

sentences.text: The standard of proof for rebutting the presumption is that of preponderance of probabilities.
(iii) To rebut the presumption, it is open for the accused to rely on evidence led by him or accused can also rely on the materials submitted by the Complainant in order to raise a probable defence.
Inference of preponderance of probabilities can be drawn not only from the materials brought on record by the parties but also by reference to the circumstances upon which they rely.

(iv) That it is not necessary for the accused to come in the witness box in support of his defence,
Sec.139 imposed an evidentiary burden and not a persuasive burden.
(v) It is not necessary for the accused to come in the witness box to support his defence.

13. In another ruling reported in AIR 2010 SC 1898 (Rangappa V/s Mohan), observed as under:-
"Existence of legally recoverable debt or liability- The presumption mandated by Section 139 of the Act does indeed include the existence of a legally enforceable debt or liability.
This is of course in the nature of a rebuttable presumption and it is open to the accused to raise a defence wherein the existence of a legally enforceable debt or liability can be contested.
However, there can be no doubt that there is an initial presumption which favours the Complainant.
Section 139 of the Act is an example of a reverse onus clause that has been included in furtherance of the legislative objective of improving the credibility of negotiable instruments.

While Section 138 of the Act specifies a strong criminal remedy in relation to the dishonour of cheques, the rebuttable presumption under Section 139, is a device to prevent undue delay in the course of litigation.

However, it must be remembered that the offence made punishable by Section 138 can be better described as a regulatory offence since the bouncing of a cheque is largely in the nature of a civil wrong whose impact is usually confined to the private parties involved in commercial transactions.

In such a scenario, the test of proportionality should guide the construction and interpretation of reverse onus clauses and the accused/ defendant cannot be expected to discharge an unduly high standard or proof.
In the absence of compelling justifications, reverse onus clauses usually impose an evidentiary burden and not a persuasive burden.
Keeping this in view, it is a settled position that when an accused has to rebut the presumption under Section 139, the standard of proof for doing so is that of 'preponderance of probabilities'.
Therefore, if the accused is able to raise a probable defence which creates doubts about the existence of a legally enforceable debt or liability, the prosecution can fail.

The accused can rely on the materials submitted by the Complainant and it is conceivable that in some cases the accused may not need to adduce evidence of his/her own."
